highlights.content: # **Two Years of LLM Progress on Data Analysis** *Nov 12, 2026: Ten older models, from GPT-4o to GPT-5.4, run through the same exam as today's.* At Plotly, we keep a close eye on model releases. Our agentic analytics products, Plotly Studio Desktop and Plotly Studio Embedded, and our open source libraries Plotly and Dash work with any model, and our customers look to us for recommendations. Since September we've run every new model through DataAnalyticsBench, our exam of 43 data analysis questions. That told us which model is best today, but not how fast things are moving. So this week we went back and ran ten older models through the same exam, with the same harness and grading: OpenAI's **GPT-4o**, **GPT-5** and **GPT-5.4**, Meta's **Llama 3.3 70B** and **Llama 4 Maverick**, **DeepSeek V3**, Google's **Gemini 2.5 Pro**, Moonshot's **Kimi K2**, and Anthropic's **Claude Opus 4.1** and **Claude Opus 4.6**. Together with the 47 models already on our board, that's 57 models released between November 2024 and November 2026. Two years ago, the best model we tested, GPT-4o, passed **20 of 43** questions. A year later, GPT-5 passed 35. Today, three models pass all 43, and GPT-6 Luna beats GPT-5's score for about a thirty-sixth of the cost. ![Data analytics benchmark scores for 57 language models by release date, from GPT-4o at 47% in November 2024 to three models at 100% in late 2026](https://plotly.com/cms/img/UrsbVpjsU8vULPYY_llm-progress-data-analysis-by-release-date.png?auto=compress&fm=webp) ## **The ten older models** **Model** **Released** **Score** **Cost per run** **Median time per question** GPT-4o Nov 2024 20 / 43 $5.83 7 seconds Llama 3.3 70B† Dec 2024 6 / 43 $6.67 5 seconds DeepSeek V3† Dec 2024 17 / 43 $0.94 27 seconds Llama 4 Maverick† Apr 2025 4 / 43 $0.25 10 seconds Gemini 2.5 Pro Jun 2025 30 / 43 $47.43 27 seconds Kimi K2† Jul 2025 30 / 43 $6.30 40 seconds Claude Opus 4.1 Aug 2025 28 / 43 $46.61 103 seconds GPT-5 Aug 2025 35 / 43 $4.67 82 seconds Claude Opus 4.6 Feb 2026 35 / 43 $15.76 32 seconds GPT-5.4 Mar 2026 34 / 43 $3.02 13 seconds † = open weights. Release dates are when each model became available on OpenRouter, which is how we ran all of them. GPT-4o is the November 2024 version. Costs are at OpenRouter's prices today, for one full run of the exam. ## **What changed** The exam has six kinds of questions, and they didn't improve at the same pace. **GPT-4o** (Nov 2024) **GPT-5** (Aug 2025) **GPT-5.4** (Mar 2026) **GPT-6.1 Sol** (Sep 2026) **Claude Fable 5.2** (Nov 2026) Analytics questions 13 / 20 19 / 20 20 / 20 20 / 20 20 / 20 Ambiguous questions 2 / 5 5 / 5 5 / 5 5 / 5 5 / 5 Impossible requests 4 / 5 5 / 5 4 / 5 5 / 5 5 / 5 Data quality 1 / 3 1 / 3 0 / 3 3 / 3 3 / 3 Statistics traps 0 / 5 3 / 5 3 / 5 5 / 5 5 / 5 Hidden needles 0 / 5 2 / 5 2 / 5 5 / 5 5 / 5 Total 20 / 43 35 / 43 34 / 43 43 / 43 43 / 43 **The straightforward analytics were mostly solved by mid-2025.** These are questions with one right number, like a regional total or a ranking with ties. GPT-4o got 13 of 20, usually losing points to small SQL mistakes: comparing dates to timestamps as text, or ending a month at midnight on its last day. By August 2025, Gemini 2.5 Pro, Kimi K2 and Claude Opus 4.1 each got 18, and GPT-5 got 19. **Judgment came next.** The ambiguous questions reward a model for asking what you mean, or saying which reading it chose, and the impossible ones reward it for saying the data can't answer the question. This lesson aims to provide an in-depth look at open source models. If you are looking for information on how proprietary models compare to open source models, go to the ["Exploring and Comparing Different LLMs" lesson](https://github.com/microsoft/generative-ai-for-beginners/blob/main/02-exploring-and-comparing-different-llms/README.md?WT.mc_id=academic-105485-koreyst). This lesson will also cover the topic of fine-tuning but a more detailed explanation can be found in the ["Fine-Tuning LLMs" lesson](https://github.com/microsoft/generative-ai-for-beginners/blob/main/18-fine-tuning/README.md?WT.mc_id=academic-105485-koreyst). - Gain an understanding of open source Models - Understanding the benefits of working with open source Models - Exploring the open models available on Hugging Face and the Microsoft Foundry model catalog Open source software has played a crucial role in the growth of technology across various fields. The Open Source Initiative (OSI) has defined [10 criteria for software](https://web.archive.org/web/20241126001143/https://opensource.org/osd?WT.mc_id=academic-105485-koreyst) to be classified as open source. The source code must be openly shared under a license approved by the OSI. While the development of LLMs has similar elements to developing software, the process is not exactly the same. This has brought much discussion in the community on the definition of open source in the context of LLMs. For a model to be aligned with the traditional definition of open source the following information should be publicly available: - Datasets used to train the model. - Full model weights as a part of the training. - The evaluation code. - The fine-tuning code. - Full model weights and training metrics. There are currently only a few models that match this criteria. The [OLMo model created by Allen Institute for Artificial Intelligence (AllenAI)](https://huggingface.co/allenai/OLMo-7B?WT.mc_id=academic-105485-koreyst) is one that fits this category. For this lesson, we will refer to the models as "open models" going forward as they may not match the criteria above at the time of writing. **Highly Customizable** - Since open models are released with detailed training information, researchers and developers can modify the model's internals. This enables the creation of highly specialized models that are fine-tuned for a specific task or area of study. Some examples of this are code generation, mathematical operations and biology. **Cost** - The cost per token for using and deploying these models is lower than that of proprietary models. When building Generative AI applications, looking at performance vs price when working with these models on your use case should be done. highlights.content: Intel and NVIDIA are two of the most widely followed semiconductor companies, yet they sit at very different points in the technology cycle. Intel is working to reinvent itself as both a chip designer and a third-party manufacturer, while NVIDIA has become the de facto engine of the AI infrastructure buildout. This stock comparison is relevant for investors weighing a high-risk turnaround story against a high-growth, higher-valuation AI leader. Traders may also find value in contrasting how each name responds to sentiment shifts, earnings surprises, and sector-wide moves. The sections below examine recent performance, growth drivers, risk factors, and relative market positioning. Intel Corporation designs and manufactures central processing units (CPUs), graphics processors, accelerators, and networking components, and it is building a foundry business to fabricate chips for outside customers. Its most recent quarterly results showed revenue rising roughly 21% year over year, led by the Data Center and AI segment, which grew strongly on demand tied to AI infrastructure. However, sentiment deteriorated after management warned that near-term revenue could fall short of expectations, citing weaker personal computer (PC) demand, supply chain disruptions, and advanced packaging constraints that limited shipments. I also checked this using Tickeron’s AI Screener to see how the stock compares to others in the industry. The company also raised significant capital through a public equity offering, which supports investment but dilutes existing shareholders. highlights.content: # From AI Assistants to Autonomous AI Agents: Are We Entering a New Era of Software Development and Business Automation? ## How Anthropic, Meta and OpenAI are moving AI beyond conversations — and what this transformation means for businesses, developers and data professionals. **By Anurag Kumar PoddarData Analyst | Business Analyst** ## Introduction: AI Is No Longer Just About Giving Answers Think about how we have traditionally used Artificial Intelligence. We ask a question, AI generates an answer. We provide information, AI summarizes it. We give it a piece of code, and it helps us improve it. We use it to generate reports, analyze data, write emails and simplify everyday tasks. But what if AI could do more than respond to our instructions? What if it could understand a business objective, break it into smaller tasks, interact with different applications, execute those tasks, identify problems and report the outcome — with appropriate human supervision? This is where **Autonomous AI Agents and Agentic AI** enter the picture. We are witnessing a significant transition in the AI ecosystem. The focus is gradually shifting from AI systems that primarily generate responses to systems that can take actions, use tools, coordinate workflows and work towards defined objectives. Recent developments from Anthropic, Meta and OpenAI provide interesting examples of this transition. From AI-assisted software development to intelligent workplace collaboration and agent-driven shopping, the direction is becoming increasingly clear. **AI is evolving from a tool that helps us work to a system that can perform parts of the work itself.** For businesses, this development deserves serious attention. ## 1. Understanding the Difference: Traditional AI vs. Agentic AI Before discussing recent developments, it is important to understand what makes an AI agent different from a traditional AI assistant. Traditional generative AI primarily focuses on understanding a prompt and generating an appropriate response. For example: - Ask AI to write SQL queries, and it generates SQL. - Ask AI to analyze sales performance, and it provides observations. - Ask AI to draft an email, and it creates the content. - Ask AI to explain a business problem, and it suggests possible solutions. Now consider an AI agent. You give it an objective: “Analyze last month’s sales performance, identify underperforming regions, compare them with the previous month, prepare a summary and notify the relevant team.” An agent-based system could potentially: 1. Retrieve the required sales data through authorized connections. 2. Analyze sales performance across regions. 3. Identify significant changes and unusual patterns. 4. Compare current performance with historical results. 5. Prepare a report with relevant observations. 6. Draft a notification for the responsible team. 7. Request approval before sending it. The important difference is that an agent can work through multiple steps rather than simply providing a response. highlights.content: # Enhancing robustness of LLM-driven multi-agent systems through randomized smoothing SciOpen **image:**  **Temporal evolution of LLM-driven UAVs’ state trajectories under adversarial scenarios.** [view more](https://www.eurekalert.org/multimedia/1164442) Credit: Hu et al./Chinese Journal of Aeronautics Multi-agent systems are becoming central to cooperative decision-making in aerospace, robotics and other safety-critical domains. Large language models (LLMs) add the flexibility to interpret instructions and reason about changing situations, but they also introduce a system-level risk. An LLM may hallucinate or accept misleading information from another agent. Once shared, that error can propagate through the network and distort the decisions of otherwise normal agents. In a recent article featured by the Chinese Journal of Aeronautics (https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cja.2025.103779), Jinwei Hu, Dr. Yi Dong and Prof. Xiaowei Huang from the University of Liverpool, together with Prof. Zhengtao Ding from the University of Manchester, developed a defence framework for LLM-driven multi-agent systems based on randomized smoothing. Originally introduced as a statistical robustness technique, randomized smoothing repeatedly evaluates a model under small, controlled perturbations and aggregates the outputs to identify decisions that remain stable under uncertainty or adversarial manipulation. "Our goal was to move beyond simply observing whether an LLM-driven group succeeds or fails," said first author Jinwei Hu. "We wanted a practical mechanism that makes unreliable information less likely to spread through the network and measures how much disturbance an agent can tolerate." The framework applies smoothing at two levels. Before accepting a neighbour's reported state, an agent queries the neighbour repeatedly with slightly perturbed inputs and combines the responses to obtain a more reliable estimate. The receiving agent then applies a second smoothing step to its own decision. A trimmed-mean aggregation removes extreme outputs, reducing the influence of malicious messages, hallucinations and inconsistent responses. The procedure only requires input-output access, so it can be applied to black-box LLM services. To control the cost of repeated LLM queries, the researchers designed a two-stage adaptive sampling strategy. A small initial sample estimates response variability. Stable responses require few additional queries, whereas high variability triggers more intensive sampling. The team also derives a certification radius describing the input perturbation an agent can withstand while remaining in the same decision region, and relates this local stability to the attenuation of misinformation across the network. The researchers evaluated the method using a ring-structured system of ten GPT-3.5-Turbo-driven agents performing a consensus-seeking task. When all agents behaved normally, their states converged smoothly. Malicious agents disrupted this process and caused persistent oscillations when no defence was present. With randomized smoothing, the normal agents returned close to the ideal consensus trajectory. The average deviation from the benign baseline was reduced by 90.24%. A three-dimensional aerospace simulation further examined ten LLM-driven UAVs maintaining a prescribed formation. False position reports prompted unnecessary avoidance manoeuvres and degraded the formation. Under the defence, the group remained substantially closer to the intended trajectory and final formation, suggesting a practical safety layer for LLM-enabled autonomous coordination. **Original Source** Jinwei Hu, Yi Dong, Zhengtao Ding, Xiaowei Huang. We ask a question, AI generates an answer. We provide information, AI summarizes it. We give it a piece of code, and it helps us improve it. We use it to generate reports, analyze data, write emails and simplify everyday tasks. But what if AI could do more than respond to our instructions? What if it could understand a business objective, break it into smaller tasks, interact with different applications, execute those tasks, identify problems and report the outcome — with appropriate human supervision? This is where **Autonomous AI Agents and Agentic AI** enter the picture. We are witnessing a significant transition in the AI ecosystem. The focus is gradually shifting from AI systems that primarily generate responses to systems that can take actions, use tools, coordinate workflows and work towards defined objectives. Recent developments from Anthropic, Meta and OpenAI provide interesting examples of this transition. From AI-assisted software development to intelligent workplace collaboration and agent-driven shopping, the direction is becoming increasingly clear. **AI is evolving from a tool that helps us work to a system that can perform parts of the work itself.** For businesses, this development deserves serious attention. ## 1. Understanding the Difference: Traditional AI vs. Agentic AI Before discussing recent developments, it is important to understand what makes an AI agent different from a traditional AI assistant. Traditional generative AI primarily focuses on understanding a prompt and generating an appropriate response. For example: - Ask AI to write SQL queries, and it generates SQL. - Ask AI to analyze sales performance, and it provides observations. - Ask AI to draft an email, and it creates the content. - Ask AI to explain a business problem, and it suggests possible solutions. Now consider an AI agent. You give it an objective: “Analyze last month’s sales performance, identify underperforming regions, compare them with the previous month, prepare a summary and notify the relevant team.” An agent-based system could potentially: 1. Retrieve the required sales data through authorized connections. 2. Analyze sales performance across regions. 3. Identify significant changes and unusual patterns. 4. Compare current performance with historical results. 5. Prepare a report with relevant observations. 6. Draft a notification for the responsible team. 7. Request approval before sending it. The important difference is that an agent can work through multiple steps rather than simply providing a response. An LLM may hallucinate or accept misleading information from another agent. Once shared, that error can propagate through the network and distort the decisions of otherwise normal agents. In a recent article featured by the Chinese Journal of Aeronautics (https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cja.2025.103779), Jinwei Hu, Dr. Yi Dong and Prof. Xiaowei Huang from the University of Liverpool, together with Prof. Zhengtao Ding from the University of Manchester, developed a defence framework for LLM-driven multi-agent systems based on randomized smoothing. Originally introduced as a statistical robustness technique, randomized smoothing repeatedly evaluates a model under small, controlled perturbations and aggregates the outputs to identify decisions that remain stable under uncertainty or adversarial manipulation. "Our goal was to move beyond simply observing whether an LLM-driven group succeeds or fails," said first author Jinwei Hu. "We wanted a practical mechanism that makes unreliable information less likely to spread through the network and measures how much disturbance an agent can tolerate." The framework applies smoothing at two levels. Before accepting a neighbour's reported state, an agent queries the neighbour repeatedly with slightly perturbed inputs and combines the responses to obtain a more reliable estimate. The receiving agent then applies a second smoothing step to its own decision. A trimmed-mean aggregation removes extreme outputs, reducing the influence of malicious messages, hallucinations and inconsistent responses. The procedure only requires input-output access, so it can be applied to black-box LLM services. To control the cost of repeated LLM queries, the researchers designed a two-stage adaptive sampling strategy. A small initial sample estimates response variability. Stable responses require few additional queries, whereas high variability triggers more intensive sampling. The team also derives a certification radius describing the input perturbation an agent can withstand while remaining in the same decision region, and relates this local stability to the attenuation of misinformation across the network. The researchers evaluated the method using a ring-structured system of ten GPT-3.5-Turbo-driven agents performing a consensus-seeking task. When all agents behaved normally, their states converged smoothly. Malicious agents disrupted this process and caused persistent oscillations when no defence was present. With randomized smoothing, the normal agents returned close to the ideal consensus trajectory. The average deviation from the benign baseline was reduced by 90.24%. A three-dimensional aerospace simulation further examined ten LLM-driven UAVs maintaining a prescribed formation. False position reports prompted unnecessary avoidance manoeuvres and degraded the formation. Under the defence, the group remained substantially closer to the intended trajectory and final formation, suggesting a practical safety layer for LLM-enabled autonomous coordination. **Original Source** Jinwei Hu, Yi Dong, Zhengtao Ding, Xiaowei Huang. AI Agents.content: ![IrisKey.ai unveils 26-gate control for autonomous AI](https://securitybrief.co.uk/uploads/story/2026/11/24/calm-ai-agent-secure-gates-blocked-access-illustration-story-325848.webp) # IrisKey.ai unveils 26-gate control for autonomous AI Wed, 25th Nov 2026 (Today) [SEAN MITCHELL Publisher](https://securitybrief.co.uk/author/sean-mitchell) ![Sean Mitchell](https://securitybrief.co.uk/rails/active_storage/representations/redirect/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsiZGF0YSI6MTYyOSwicHVyIjoiYmxvYl9pZCJ9fQ==--a929a91c2a04d9af95ed98b14ed4d405bc70c1a7/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsiZGF0YSI6eyJmb3JtYXQiOiJ3ZWJwIiwicmVzaXplX3RvX2ZpbGwiOlsxNjAsMTYwXSwicXVhbGl0eSI6ODV9LCJwdXIiOiJ2YXJpYXRpb24ifX0=--89ddf5e6765c65a563c2258053e9d33c05d195da/IMG_3092.webp) IrisKey.ai has introduced a 26-gate governance architecture for autonomous AI systems. The Coventry-based company said the design is intended to enforce authority before AI agents carry out consequential actions. The proposed, patent-pending system is designed to separate what an AI system can do from what it is allowed to do. According to IrisKey.ai, the framework would verify authority, control delegated permissions and support the withdrawal of access when authorisation changes. The move reflects a broader debate in the technology industry as AI tools shift from producing information to taking actions inside financial platforms, business software, digital infrastructure and autonomous machines. That change has raised questions about how organisations can ensure an AI agent does not exceed the permissions it has been given. Existing AI governance has largely focused on ethics, compliance, risk management and human oversight. IrisKey.ai argues that these measures alone do not provide a technical mechanism to stop an unauthorised action once an autonomous system is operating. **Authority checks** The 26-gate concept is intended to create a structured series of checks before execution. These are designed to address several issues, including whether authority can be verified before an action takes place, whether delegated permissions remain within defined limits, and whether revoked access can be prevented from being used. IrisKey.ai said the architecture is intended to work across different AI models, software environments and operational settings, although it has not disclosed the detailed design because the work sits within its intellectual property programme. It said the architecture is not meant to replace cybersecurity systems or regulatory governance, but to sit between AI decision-making and execution. Adam McCrum, Founder at IrisKey.ai, said the rise of more autonomous systems had exposed a gap between policy and technical control. "Artificial intelligence is becoming increasingly capable, but capability and authority are two very different things," said Adam McCrum, Founder at IrisKey.ai. "We are building systems that can reason, make decisions, communicate with other agents and execute actions across digital environments. Yet we still need to answer a fundamental question: what technically prevents an AI system from performing an action it was never authorised to carry out?" He said the issue becomes more acute when AI agents interact with other systems or receive delegated permissions across multiple operational environments. In those cases, the question is not only what the system has the technical means to do, but whether the action remains valid under the authority originally granted. "A governance policy cannot physically stop an unauthorised API call. A compliance dashboard cannot guarantee that a revoked permission has stopped being used. As AI moves into real-world operations, we need technical enforcement that is designed into the architecture itself." **Industry uses** The company pointed to financial services, healthcare, industrial systems, transport, defence and public-sector operations as areas where enforcement of AI permissions could be significant. AI Agents.content: AI is becoming ever more powerful, but there is more to it than building better and larger models and improving the responses of chatbots. Developers are finding new ways to customise AI agents, equipping them with special instructions and abilities that change how they approach different tasks. Ponytail, an open-source skill that helps an AI coding agent behave more like an experienced developer, is one such AI customisation example. It’s part of a blossoming ecosystem of [AI agent skills](https://em360tech.com/tech-articles/what-ai-agent-future-machine-learning-explained). Skills like this can add additional knowledge, workflows and capabilities to existing artificial intelligence (AI) systems. Some are targeted at improving the software development process, others are seeking to solve specific problems, such as making AI-generated websites more appealing or helping agents understand complicated codebases. ![em360tech image](https://em360tech.com/sites/default/files/styles/cover_image/public/2026-11/em360tech_ai-agent-skills_header_header-combined.jpg.webp?h=303d4aa7&itok=_u0mL3he) These developments are important because they show how the customisation of AI is progressing. Instead of always depending on more powerful models, programmers are beginning to give existing agents more specialised ways of working. ## What Are AI Agent Skills? Before we examine the examples, it’s useful to explain what a skill for an agent actually does. An AI agent is a [system that can use tools](https://em360tech.com/podcasts/friend-or-foe-which-ai-agents-should-your-website-le), follow instructions, and carry out tasks with varying degrees of independence. But even capable agents may have difficulty with some workflows or not have the context to be effective. Skills solve this problem by providing an agent with additional instructions, resources and sometimes scripts to help it perform a particular activity. Take a programmer’s assistant for instance, it can write programs but may not necessarily follow a particular development methodology or understand the design principles to produce a well-crafted website. That one special skill can provide that added guidance. In October 2025 Anthropic launched [its Agent Skills system](https://claude.com/resources/articles/skills), which it describes as organised sets of instructions, scripts and resources an agent can load on demand. Later, it was developed into an open standard which supports multiple AI platforms. For AI agents this means that more and more the model can be adapted to fit new needs without having to create a new model from scratch. Here are seven weird AI agent capabilities and tools worth knowing about: ## 7 Unusual AI Agent Skills and Tools ### 1. Ponytail: Teaching AI agents to write less code SIMPLICITY AND CODE OPTIMISATION [AI coding assistants](https://em360tech.com/tech-articles/ai-agents-test-data-infrastructure) sometimes complicate simple things. A request to add a simple feature to a website, for example, could result in extra libraries, lengthy code, and a feature that was never necessary to begin with. [Ponytail addresses this problem](https://ponytail.dev/) by encouraging coding agents to think like what its creator describes as the “laziest senior developer in the room”. This open-source skill encourages the agent to search for existing solutions before writing a new program. Its main purpose is to reuse existing functionality, use standard libraries, and make as few changes as possible to accomplish a task. For example, instead of installing an extra library to create a date picker, an agent might first ask whether a native HTML date input would suffice. However, this is more a question of reducing unnecessary complexity than of cutting corners. The skill also encourages proper testing, security checking, input validation and error handling. **Why it’s interesting:** Ponytail shows how a tiny set of instructions can change how an AI agent builds software. LLMs.content: # **Two Years of LLM Progress on Data Analysis** *Nov 12, 2026: Ten older models, from GPT-4o to GPT-5.4, run through the same exam as today's.* At Plotly, we keep a close eye on model releases. Our agentic analytics products, Plotly Studio Desktop and Plotly Studio Embedded, and our open source libraries Plotly and Dash work with any model, and our customers look to us for recommendations. Since September we've run every new model through DataAnalyticsBench, our exam of 43 data analysis questions. That told us which model is best today, but not how fast things are moving. So this week we went back and ran ten older models through the same exam, with the same harness and grading: OpenAI's **GPT-4o**, **GPT-5** and **GPT-5.4**, Meta's **Llama 3.3 70B** and **Llama 4 Maverick**, **DeepSeek V3**, Google's **Gemini 2.5 Pro**, Moonshot's **Kimi K2**, and Anthropic's **Claude Opus 4.1** and **Claude Opus 4.6**. Together with the 47 models already on our board, that's 57 models released between November 2024 and November 2026. Two years ago, the best model we tested, GPT-4o, passed **20 of 43** questions. A year later, GPT-5 passed 35. Today, three models pass all 43, and GPT-6 Luna beats GPT-5's score for about a thirty-sixth of the cost. ![Data analytics benchmark scores for 57 language models by release date, from GPT-4o at 47% in November 2024 to three models at 100% in late 2026](https://plotly.com/cms/img/UrsbVpjsU8vULPYY_llm-progress-data-analysis-by-release-date.png?auto=compress&fm=webp) ## **The ten older models** **Model** **Released** **Score** **Cost per run** **Median time per question** GPT-4o Nov 2024 20 / 43 $5.83 7 seconds Llama 3.3 70B† Dec 2024 6 / 43 $6.67 5 seconds DeepSeek V3† Dec 2024 17 / 43 $0.94 27 seconds Llama 4 Maverick† Apr 2025 4 / 43 $0.25 10 seconds Gemini 2.5 Pro Jun 2025 30 / 43 $47.43 27 seconds Kimi K2† Jul 2025 30 / 43 $6.30 40 seconds Claude Opus 4.1 Aug 2025 28 / 43 $46.61 103 seconds GPT-5 Aug 2025 35 / 43 $4.67 82 seconds Claude Opus 4.6 Feb 2026 35 / 43 $15.76 32 seconds GPT-5.4 Mar 2026 34 / 43 $3.02 13 seconds † = open weights. Release dates are when each model became available on OpenRouter, which is how we ran all of them. GPT-4o is the November 2024 version. Costs are at OpenRouter's prices today, for one full run of the exam. ## **What changed** The exam has six kinds of questions, and they didn't improve at the same pace. **GPT-4o** (Nov 2024) **GPT-5** (Aug 2025) **GPT-5.4** (Mar 2026) **GPT-6.1 Sol** (Sep 2026) **Claude Fable 5.2** (Nov 2026) Analytics questions 13 / 20 19 / 20 20 / 20 20 / 20 20 / 20 Ambiguous questions 2 / 5 5 / 5 5 / 5 5 / 5 5 / 5 Impossible requests 4 / 5 5 / 5 4 / 5 5 / 5 5 / 5 Data quality 1 / 3 1 / 3 0 / 3 3 / 3 3 / 3 Statistics traps 0 / 5 3 / 5 3 / 5 5 / 5 5 / 5 Hidden needles 0 / 5 2 / 5 2 / 5 5 / 5 5 / 5 Total 20 / 43 35 / 43 34 / 43 43 / 43 43 / 43 **The straightforward analytics were mostly solved by mid-2025.** These are questions with one right number, like a regional total or a ranking with ties. GPT-4o got 13 of 20, usually losing points to small SQL mistakes: comparing dates to timestamps as text, or ending a month at midnight on its last day. By August 2025, Gemini 2.5 Pro, Kimi K2 and Claude Opus 4.1 each got 18, and GPT-5 got 19. **Judgment came next.** The ambiguous questions reward a model for asking what you mean, or saying which reading it chose, and the impossible ones reward it for saying the data can't answer the question. In late 2024 the models mostly guessed. By the summer of 2025, Kimi K2 and GPT-5 got all ten. **The traps took longest.** Three kinds of question reward a model for checking its own work: data quality problems hidden in the warehouse, statistics traps where the obvious conclusion is wrong, and hidden patterns that only show up if you slice the data the right way. We build Annotated Stepwise Clinical rEasoning for NaturalisTic Diagnosis (ASCENT), a clinician-annotated benchmark and training resource of 3,078 stepwise problems derived from MedQA-USMLE that decomposes each vignette into EMR-aligned steps (Findings, Impression, supporting Rationale), enabling evaluation of intermediate reasoning under incomplete information. Experiments and training with ASCENT revealed insights into how current LLMs handle stepwise diagnostic reasoning. Even strong reasoning models that perform well on MedQA-USMLE leave substantial headroom on ASCENT, and general-purpose frontier models trail further—exposing a persistent gap between fully informed and stepwise diagnosis. Fine-tuning Qwen2.5-7B and 32B on ASCENT yields measurable F1 gains over both pre-trained and HuatuoGPT-o1 CoT-trained baselines, with gains driven primarily by precision. Complementary robustness analyses (counterfactual perturbation, format-vs-content control, judge agreement, and rollout) further show that ASCENT-fine-tuned models rely on the diagnostic content of prior impressions rather than imitating their output format, while error propagation under rollout remains a key challenge for clinical deployment. † †volume: 333 † †year: 2026 † †submitted: LEAVE UNSET † †published: LEAVE UNSET † †workshop: Conference on Health, Inference, and Learning (CHIL) 2026 #### Data and Code Availability This paper uses the MedQA-USMLE benchmark dataset, which is available on the HuggingFace Datasets repository ([Jin et al., 2020](#bib.bib6)). LLMs.content: [Artificial Intelligence](https://singularityhub.com/category/artificial-intelligence/) # This AI Tweaks LLM Neural Networks Like a Gene Editor OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra looked at raw numbers behind neural networks to decipher what they do, repair faults, and write working AI models from scratch. ![Two spherical networks of lighted nodes side by side](https://singularityhub.com/uploads/2026/11/lighted-spherical-networks-and-nodes.jpeg?auto=webp&auto=webp&optimize=high&quality=70&width=1440) Image Credit Nick Fewings on Unsplash Share [In a preprint](https://www.alphaxiv.org/abs/2611.weight-space-programming) that recently spread like wildfire, researchers at MIT reported using GPT-6 Astra, a frontier large language model (LLM) developed by OpenAI, to probe the strengths of connections—called weights—that govern how other AI models work. In a series of tests, Astra interpreted weights well enough to decipher what different parts of a model do, hunt down failure points, and even write new models from scratch, all without conventionally training the target networks. In one experiment, Astra found that a small reasoning model got stuck in repetitive loops when tackling tough math problems. By tweaking just 0.016 percent of its weights, Astra vastly improved the model’s scores. In another, it diagnosed a faulty neural network controlling a virtual car and repaired it with a few targeted edits. That’s not to say Astra can pinpoint the role of every part in a given AI model. But like a seasoned mechanic tinkering with an unfamiliar engine, it can suss out problems without knowing exactly what every nut and bolt does. “This is cool as heck!” [wrote](https://x.com/Yuchenj_UW/status/2117353356226379964) Yuchen Jin, co-founder of [Hyperbolic Labs](https://www.hyperbolic.ai/) who was not involved in the research on X. “Imagine using a large LLM to directly edit a smaller model's weights and dramatically improve its capabilities.” The team released complete logs of every reported experiment, allowing others to evaluate and build upon the work. [Scientists](https://www.turing.ac.uk/news/publications/replicating-weight-space-programming-writing-and-reading-neural-network-weights) at The Alan Turing Institute replicated and extended the results, cautiously concluding that “it is a promising but early tool for \[AI] interpretability.” [Another team](https://csinva.io/weight-space-programming-autoresearch/analyze/toy_examples/report.html), led by [Voyage AI’s](https://www.voyageai.com/) Chandan Singh, used Anthropic’s Claude to write small transformers from scratch that could solve a variety of basic math problems, reaching nearly perfect accuracy within three attempts. “For anyone questioning whether this post is overhyped, I think they are actually \*underselling* the approach,” Singh [wrote](https://x.com/csinva/status/2117338122694381595) on X. ## What’s in the Box? Artificial neural networks form the backbone of today’s most sophisticated AI models. Loosely inspired by the brain, they’re made of layers of units called “neurons” with mathematical weights governing the strength of their connections. Models aren’t ready to go out of the box. A network consumes a trove of examples, learning by trial and error. Each mistake tweaks its weights, gradually nudging the model towards success. The LLMs powering ChatGPT and Gemini all rely on this basic process, but on a vast scale. AI researchers have [developed ways](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3700439) to speed up training, but it remains a costly computational slog and an energy hog. And with millions or billions of weights changed along the way, the resulting networks are notoriously incomprehensible. Scientists have been trying to [pry open AI’s “black box”](https://singularityhub.com/2026/02/23/researchers-break-open-ais-black-box-and-use-what-they-find-to-control-it/) for years. Open Source AI.content: ![Open Source Models](https://github.com/microsoft/generative-ai-for-beginners/raw/main/16-open-source-models/images/16-lesson-banner.png?WT.mc_id=academic-105485-koreyst) The world of open-source LLMs is exciting and constantly evolving. This lesson aims to provide an in-depth look at open source models. If you are looking for information on how proprietary models compare to open source models, go to the ["Exploring and Comparing Different LLMs" lesson](https://github.com/microsoft/generative-ai-for-beginners/blob/main/02-exploring-and-comparing-different-llms/README.md?WT.mc_id=academic-105485-koreyst). This lesson will also cover the topic of fine-tuning but a more detailed explanation can be found in the ["Fine-Tuning LLMs" lesson](https://github.com/microsoft/generative-ai-for-beginners/blob/main/18-fine-tuning/README.md?WT.mc_id=academic-105485-koreyst). - Gain an understanding of open source Models - Understanding the benefits of working with open source Models - Exploring the open models available on Hugging Face and the Microsoft Foundry model catalog Open source software has played a crucial role in the growth of technology across various fields. The Open Source Initiative (OSI) has defined [10 criteria for software](https://web.archive.org/web/20241126001143/https://opensource.org/osd?WT.mc_id=academic-105485-koreyst) to be classified as open source. The source code must be openly shared under a license approved by the OSI. While the development of LLMs has similar elements to developing software, the process is not exactly the same. This has brought much discussion in the community on the definition of open source in the context of LLMs. For a model to be aligned with the traditional definition of open source the following information should be publicly available: - Datasets used to train the model. - Full model weights as a part of the training. - The evaluation code. - The fine-tuning code. - Full model weights and training metrics. There are currently only a few models that match this criteria. The [OLMo model created by Allen Institute for Artificial Intelligence (AllenAI)](https://huggingface.co/allenai/OLMo-7B?WT.mc_id=academic-105485-koreyst) is one that fits this category. For this lesson, we will refer to the models as "open models" going forward as they may not match the criteria above at the time of writing. **Highly Customizable** - Since open models are released with detailed training information, researchers and developers can modify the model's internals. This enables the creation of highly specialized models that are fine-tuned for a specific task or area of study. Some examples of this are code generation, mathematical operations and biology. **Cost** - The cost per token for using and deploying these models is lower than that of proprietary models. When building Generative AI applications, looking at performance vs price when working with these models on your use case should be done. Source: Artificial Analysis![Model Cost](https://github.com/microsoft/generative-ai-for-beginners/raw/main/16-open-source-models/images/model-price.png?WT.mc_id=academic-105485-koreyst) **Flexibility** - Working with open models enables you to be flexible in terms of using different models or combining them. An example of this is the [HuggingChat Assistants](https://huggingface.co/chat?WT.mc_id=academic-105485-koreyst) where a user can select the model being used directly in the user interface: ![Choose Model](https://github.com/microsoft/generative-ai-for-beginners/raw/main/16-open-source-models/images/choose-model.png?WT.mc_id=academic-105485-koreyst) [LLama2](https://huggingface.co/meta-llama?WT.mc_id=academic-105485-koreyst), developed by Meta is an open model that is optimized for chat based applications. Infra & Chips.content: Intel and NVIDIA are two of the most widely followed semiconductor companies, yet they sit at very different points in the technology cycle. Intel is working to reinvent itself as both a chip designer and a third-party manufacturer, while NVIDIA has become the de facto engine of the AI infrastructure buildout. This stock comparison is relevant for investors weighing a high-risk turnaround story against a high-growth, higher-valuation AI leader. Traders may also find value in contrasting how each name responds to sentiment shifts, earnings surprises, and sector-wide moves. The sections below examine recent performance, growth drivers, risk factors, and relative market positioning. Intel Corporation designs and manufactures central processing units (CPUs), graphics processors, accelerators, and networking components, and it is building a foundry business to fabricate chips for outside customers. Its most recent quarterly results showed revenue rising roughly 21% year over year, led by the Data Center and AI segment, which grew strongly on demand tied to AI infrastructure. However, sentiment deteriorated after management warned that near-term revenue could fall short of expectations, citing weaker personal computer (PC) demand, supply chain disruptions, and advanced packaging constraints that limited shipments. A bright spot arrived when Intel announced its first external customer for its 18A advanced process node, a milestone for its foundry ambitions. The company also raised significant capital through a public equity offering, which supports investment but dilutes existing shareholders. Net-net, Intel is a story of credible progress offset by execution risk and uneven end-market demand. NVIDIA Corporation designs graphics processing units (GPUs) and full-stack accelerated computing platforms that power data centers, AI training and inference, and high-performance computing. Its latest quarter reflected continued outsized demand, with revenue up sharply year over year and data center sales driving nearly all of the growth. Management also raised its forward growth outlook, signaling confidence that AI infrastructure spending remains robust. The episode introduced governance and regulatory overhang—including scrutiny over advanced-chip exports to China—alongside debate about valuation. Even so, NVIDIA's fundamental momentum, expanding data center revenue, and central role in AI infrastructure keep it at the heart of the sector narrative. Infra & Chips.content: **NEWS ANALYSIS** Jensen Huang is back as Nvidia CEO, and as the company moves beyond GPUs into agent security and infrastructure, enterprises must decide how much of their AI stack to hand over to the chip giant. Infra & Chips.content: # Behind the Headlines Every semiconductor announcement has two stories — the one on the surface, and the real story grounded in physical evidence, market data, and 35 years of reverse engineering. This is where you find the second one. ## AI compute, capital markets *Two stories about where the real risk in the AI buildout actually sits. NVIDIA's biggest long-term threat isn't a rival chipmaker; it's hyperscalers deciding they no longer need NVIDIA's margins, and the same hyperscalers' capex is increasingly funded by debt and equity rather than their own cash, changing what that spending actually signals about commitment and risk.* ## NVIDIA’s Succession Crisis Just Revealed a China Revenue Stream It Never Disclosed. NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang resigned on November 12, 2026, following revelations of multiple extramarital affairs, including at least one with an NVIDIA subordinate and one with a woman U.S. officials have linked to Chinese intelligence services. After eleven days with CFO Colette Kress serving as interim CEO, NVIDIA's board reversed course and reinstated Huang on November 23, following a public campaign from prominent tech and political figures, including President Trump, who said he personally “convinced” the board. Coverage has largely treated the reinstatement, and NVIDIA's roughly 30% single-day stock surge on the news, as the resolution of the crisis. The more consequential finding sits underneath the personal scandal. After 33 years with Huang as its only CEO, NVIDIA never established a clear succession plan, a gap the board's reversal papers over rather than resolves. That governance gap is now moot in the narrowest sense — Huang is back — but the reinstatement settles the leadership question without resolving any of the substantive ones the scandal actually raised. If anything, those questions have gotten louder: Senate Banking's ranking Democrat, Elizabeth Warren, has stated that Huang, NVIDIA's board, and the company still owe Congress answers about export-control compliance, and at least one House member is calling for Huang to testify under oath, with Senate Democrats separately vowing a formal investigation into both NVIDIA and the administration's role in bringing him back. That role is no longer alleged but confirmed: President Trump has said publicly that he personally pushed the board to reinstate Huang. That involvement may cut against NVIDIA rather than for it — Baird's own read of the reinstatement called it a potential “worst-case scenario” for China specifically, on the reasoning that a politically compromised Huang makes it harder for NVIDIA to keep credibly lobbying Washington against tighter export controls, even as the same reinstatement removes the deeper leadership-vacuum risk markets had been pricing in days earlier. The more surprising development is financial rather than personal: Huang's relationship with Alice Huang (the woman allegedly linked to Chinese intelligence services) has reportedly intersected with chip sales routed into China through a company called Megaspeed, suggesting NVIDIA's real addressable China market was larger than what appeared in its own public filings — a detail now drawing regulatory scrutiny that could undercut the export-control credibility NVIDIA has spent years building in Washington. None of this threatens NVIDIA's near-term operating reality: fiscal third-quarter revenue hit $115.8 billion, up 103% year-over-year, and its relationship with TSMC is institutional rather than personal, so production and roadmap continuity aren't seriously at risk from the leadership question alone. Infra & Chips.title: Nvidia sellers seek buyers after U.S. China AI rule: Sources
Infra & Chips.titleZh: Nvidia sellers seek buyers after U.S. China AI rule: Sources
Infra & Chips.content: [Nvidia](https://www.cnbc.com/quotes/NVDA/) chip sellers are seeking new buyers for the semiconductor giant's hardware, three people told CNBC, after the Trump administration tightened rules to curb Chinese companies' remote access to the most advanced artificial-intelligence systems. Companies have put an unusually high volume of Nvidia graphics processing units, or GPUs, on the market since new measures restricting Chinese companies renting access to advanced Nvidia chips were announced on Nov. 16, the people said. Jack Duhamel, president of AI infrastructure marketplace GPU Mart, and two people familiar with the matter told CNBC the surge in GPUs for sale was directly attributable to the new rule. Duhamel added that one company looking to sell Nvidia chips told GPU Mart the sale was related to the new rule. The two people said it appeared chip sellers were seeking to offload them because they were originally for use in data centers in which Chinese companies would rent access. They asked not to be named because they were discussing private information. The Department of Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security, or BIS, announced an [interim final rule](https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/16/nvidia-commerce-china-lutnick.html) as part of a clampdown on Chinese companies bypassing export controls, which effectively ban the sale of the most advanced Nvidia chips to China, by accessing them remotely in overseas data centers. The rule came into effect on Nov. 19. Deals to find buyers for thousands of B300 GPUs, one of Nvidia's most advanced offerings, have been floated since the rule was announced, said Duhamel and one of the people. Nvidia declined to comment. BIS did not immediately respond to a request for comment. ## Scrutiny over Chinese access to Nvidia chips Nvidia has been facing increasing scrutiny from U.S. lawmakers over Chinese companies' access to its advanced chips. The chip giant warned its customers that the proposed Remote Access Security Act — which has passed the House of Representatives but is yet to pass the Senate — would give the U.S. government broader authority to control access to cloud services, potentially exposing both parties to "legal action," [sources previously told CNBC.](https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/17/nvidia-china-cloud-ai-chip-access.html) In July, the U.S. accused a Chinese AI lab, [Moonshot AI](https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/05/moonshot-ai-nvidia-chips-europe-china.html), of accessing Nvidia chips via a facility in Thailand. CNBC reported on Nov. 5 that the company had [sought access to the chips](https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/05/moonshot-ai-nvidia-chips-europe-china.html) via data centers in Europe. ![U.S. Trade Rep. Greer on new tariff proposals: Targeted tariffs in response to excess capacity](https://image.cnbcfm.com/api/v1/image/108559246-17956146901795614684-49853581115-1080pnbcnews.jpg?v=1795614689&w=750&h=422&vtcrop=y) U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer told CNBC's "Squawk Box" on Wednesday that the new rule announced last week was intended to close "loopholes." "For a long time, we have not allowed the sale of Blackwell chips, which are the highest AI chips or similar chips to China directly," he said. "Some rules were issued by the Commerce Department last week to close off indirect access, either smuggling through places like Southeast Asia or remote access from data centers in third countries." During Nvidia's third-quarter earnings call on Nov. 17, then-interim CEO Colette Kress said the company was still studying the controls, but expected performance to remain strong because demand for chips far exceeded supply.
